items.prompt: To show how the temperature of water changes over 30 minutes, the best graph is a ___ graph.
hints: Time and temperature are both numbers that change smoothly.
This graph joins plotted points to show a change over time.
Bar charts suit separate groups. Think of the graph that joins dots instead.
items.explanation: A line graph shows how a measurement changes over time. The points are plotted and joined, so you can see the pattern and read values in between.

items.prompt: Sinta draws a line graph of her plant's height against time. Which goes on the horizontal axis?

options.why: Height is what she measures, so it goes on the vertical axis.
The name does not change, so it cannot go on an axis.
Colour is not measured with numbers here.

hints: The variable you choose or change goes on the horizontal axis.
The variable you measure goes on the vertical axis.
Ask which one Sinta decides in advance: the days she measures on, or the height.
items.explanation: Time is the variable Sinta chooses, so it goes on the horizontal (x) axis. The height she measures goes on the vertical (y) axis.

items.prompt: Mei Lin measures the temperature of a cup of tea every 5 minutes. By how many degrees did the tea cool in the first 10 minutes?

figure.caption: Cooling tea
head: Time (minutes)
Temperature (°C)
figure.alt: Table: at 0 minutes the tea is 80 °C, at 5 minutes 64 °C, at 10 minutes 52 °C, at 15 minutes 44 °C, at 20 minutes 38 °C and at 25 minutes 34 °C.

hints: Find the temperature at 0 minutes and at 10 minutes.
Cooling means the temperature went down, so find the difference.
Subtract the temperature at 10 minutes from the starting temperature.
items.explanation: The tea started at 80 °C and was 52 °C after 10 minutes. 80 − 52 = 28, so it cooled by 28 °C.

items.prompt: Look at Mei Lin's results for her cooling tea. What pattern do they show?

figure.caption: Cooling tea
head: Time (minutes)
Temperature (°C)
figure.alt: Table: at 0 minutes the tea is 80 °C, at 5 minutes 64 °C, at 10 minutes 52 °C, at 15 minutes 44 °C, at 20 minutes 38 °C and at 25 minutes 34 °C.

options.text: The tea cools by the same amount every 5 minutes.
options.why: It drops 16 °C in the first 5 minutes but only 4 °C in the last 5 minutes.

options.text: The tea gets hotter over time.
options.why: The temperatures go down, not up.

options.text: The tea cools quickly at first, then more slowly.
The tea stops cooling after 10 minutes.
options.why: The temperature keeps falling, just more slowly.

hints: Work out how much the tea cools in each 5-minute step.
Compare the first drop with the last drop.
Find the drop from 0 to 5 minutes, then from 20 to 25 minutes.
items.explanation: The tea cools by 16 °C in the first 5 minutes but by only 4 °C in the last 5 minutes. It cools quickly at first, then more slowly as it gets closer to room temperature.

items.prompt: Leo plots these results on a line graph. Use the pattern to estimate the plant's height on day 6.

figure.caption: Height of a bean plant
head: Day
Height (cm)
figure.alt: Table: on day 0 the plant is 2 cm tall, on day 4 it is 6 cm, on day 8 it is 10 cm and on day 12 it is 14 cm.

hints: Look at how much the plant grows every 4 days.
Day 6 is halfway between day 4 and day 8.
Find the height halfway between the heights on day 4 and day 8.
items.explanation: The plant grows 4 cm every 4 days, which is 1 cm a day. Day 6 is halfway between day 4 (6 cm) and day 8 (10 cm), so the height is about 8 cm.

items.prompt: Omar hangs masses on a spring and measures how far it stretches. Which result in his table is anomalous?

figure.caption: Stretching a spring
head: Mass added (g)
Stretch (cm)
figure.alt: Table: 100 g stretches the spring 2 cm, 200 g stretches it 4 cm, 300 g 9 cm, 400 g 8 cm and 500 g 10 cm.

options.why: 2 cm fits the pattern of 2 cm for every 100 g.
8 cm fits the pattern of 2 cm for every 100 g.
10 cm fits the pattern of 2 cm for every 100 g.

hints: An anomalous result does not fit the pattern of the others.
Most results go up by the same amount for every 100 g.
Use the pattern to work out the stretch you would expect for 300 g.
items.explanation: The spring stretches 2 cm for every 100 g, so 300 g should give 6 cm, not 9 cm. This anomalous result should be measured again.

items.prompt: Rizky rolls one ball once on carpet and once on wood. It rolls further on wood. He says balls always roll less far on rough surfaces. Why is his evidence weak?

options.text: He tested only one ball, once on each of two surfaces.
He should have used a forcemeter.
options.why: The problem is the number of tests, not the equipment.

options.text: Wood and carpet are both rough.
options.why: Carpet is rougher than wood, so the comparison makes sense. He just needs more results.

options.text: Balls always roll the same distance.
options.why: The distance does change with the surface. His evidence is just too small to say always.

hints: The word always makes a very strong claim.
Think about how many results he collected.
Ask what he should do before saying always.
items.explanation: One ball rolled once on each of two surfaces is too little evidence for a rule about all balls and all surfaces. He should repeat the test and try more balls and surfaces.

items.prompt: Draw a line graph of Mei Lin's cooling tea results. Label both axes with units, use even scales, plot the points and join them.

figure.caption: Cooling tea
head: Time (minutes)
Temperature (°C)
figure.alt: Table: at 0 minutes the tea is 80 °C, at 5 minutes 64 °C, at 10 minutes 52 °C, at 15 minutes 44 °C, at 20 minutes 38 °C and at 25 minutes 34 °C.

criteria.label: Puts time on the horizontal axis, with units
Puts temperature on the vertical axis, with units
Uses even scales on both axes
Joins the points with a smooth curve or straight lines

hints: Choose scales so that the graph fills most of the grid.
Plot each point carefully, then join them.
items.explanation: Time goes on the horizontal axis and temperature on the vertical axis, each with an even scale and units. The plotted points make a curve that falls steeply at first, then levels off.

items.prompt: Jane Goodall spent many years watching wild chimpanzees in Tanzania. She saw them use sticks to catch termites. Which scientific skill was most important in her work?

options.why: She studied wild chimpanzees in their habitat, so she watched them instead of testing them in a laboratory.
Her discoveries came from watching behaviour, not from temperatures.

options.text: careful observation over a long time

options.why: Circuits have nothing to do with studying chimpanzees.

hints: She did not change anything about the chimpanzees' lives.
Her discoveries came from what she saw them do in the wild.
Ask which skill lets a scientist learn without doing an experiment.
items.explanation: Jane Goodall learned by observing chimpanzees closely for many years in their natural habitat. Careful observation showed that chimpanzees make and use tools.

items.prompt: In a town, ice cream sales and cases of sunburn both rise in the same months. Does eating ice cream cause sunburn?

options.text: Yes, because the two rise together.
options.why: Rising together does not prove that one causes the other.

options.text: No. Hot, sunny weather makes both go up.
Yes, because ice cream makes skin weaker.
options.why: There is no evidence for this. Sunny weather is the link.

options.text: No, because sunburn only happens in winter.
options.why: Sunburn is most common in sunny months.

hints: Two things can rise together because a third thing causes both.
Think about the weather in the months when both go up.
Ask what makes people buy ice cream and also makes people get sunburnt.
items.explanation: Hot, sunny weather makes people buy more ice cream and also causes more sunburn. The two rise together, but one does not cause the other.

items.prompt: Read the graph. What was the temperature of the water at 10 minutes?
hints: Find 10 on the horizontal axis.
Go up to the point, then across.
Read the value on the vertical axis.
items.explanation: At 10 minutes the point is at 50 °C.

figure.alt: A line graph titled Cooling water. The horizontal axis is time in minutes from 0 to 25 and the vertical axis is temperature in degrees Celsius from 0 to 100. Six points are joined by a line that falls steeply at first and then flattens.

items.prompt: Look at the graph. Between which times did the water cool the fastest?

options.why: The line is nearly flat there, so it cooled slowly.
It cooled less here than at the start.
The line is flatter here.

hints: The steepest part of the line shows the biggest change.
Compare the fall in each 5 minute step.
Check the first step.
items.explanation: The water cooled by 18 °C in the first 5 minutes, which is the steepest part of the line.

figure.alt: A line graph titled Cooling water. The horizontal axis is time in minutes from 0 to 25 and the vertical axis is temperature in degrees Celsius from 0 to 100. Six points are joined by a line that falls steeply at first and then flattens.

items.prompt: Tap the point that looks anomalous in the plant growth graph.

figure.alt: A line graph of plant height against day. The horizontal axis is the day from 0 to 6 and the vertical axis is height in centimetres from 0 to 20. Points rise in a steady pattern from day 1, but one point is far higher than the points on each side of it.

hints: An anomalous result does not fit the pattern.
The other points rise by about the same amount each day.
One point is much higher than its neighbours.
items.explanation: The point on day 4 is far above the steady pattern, so it is anomalous.

items.prompt: Label the parts of the graph.

figure.alt: A line graph titled Cooling water. The horizontal axis is time in minutes from 0 to 25 and the vertical axis is temperature in degrees Celsius from 0 to 100. Six points are joined by a line that falls steeply at first and then flattens.

hints: The title tells you what the graph is about.
Axis labels say what is measured and the unit.
A plotted point is shown by a dot.
items.explanation: The title says what the graph is about, the axis labels say what was measured, and each dot is a plotted point.

items.prompt: Read the graph and complete the table.
head: Day
Height (cm)
hints: Find the day on the horizontal axis.
Go up to the point.
Read across to the height scale.
items.explanation: On day 2 the height was 7 cm and on day 4 it was 14 cm.

figure.alt: A line graph of a bean seedling. The horizontal axis is the day from 0 to 5 and the vertical axis is height in centimetres from 0 to 20. The line climbs from the left to the right and levels off a little at the end.

items.prompt: Which of these is best shown on a bar chart?

options.text: the temperature of water every minute
options.why: Change over time suits a line graph.

options.text: the height of a plant each day
options.why: Change over time suits a line graph.

options.text: the number of pupils choosing each pet
the distance a car travels each second
options.why: This is a continuous measure.

hints: Bar charts show separate categories.
Line graphs show change over time.
Which one counts different groups?
items.explanation: Pets are separate categories, so a bar chart suits them. Changes over time are shown with line graphs.

items.prompt: A bean plant is 6 cm tall on day 2 and 14 cm tall on day 4. It grows at a steady rate. How tall will it be on day 3?
hints: Find the height halfway between the two.
Work out the change between day 2 and day 4.
Add half the change to 6.
items.explanation: The plant grows 8 cm in 2 days, so 4 cm per day. 6 + 4 = 10 cm.

items.prompt: Omar hangs masses on a spring. Which pattern do the results show?

options.why: 10, 12, 14 is not doubling.

options.text: The length goes up by 2 cm for each extra 50 g.
The length goes up by 2 cm for each extra 100 g.
options.why: Check the mass step again. Each row adds 50 g, not 100 g.
The length changes.

hints: Find the change between each pair.
Check the mass step and the length step.
Compare the same steps.
items.explanation: Each 50 g added makes the spring 2 cm longer.

head: Mass (g)
Length (cm)
figure.alt: Table of spring length. 0 g gives 10 cm, 50 g gives 12 cm, 100 g gives 14 cm, 150 g gives 16 cm and 200 g gives 18 cm.

items.prompt: Rina tests three paper towels once each. Towel A soaks up 20 ml, B 35 ml and C 28 ml. Which conclusion is supported?

options.text: Towel B is the best for every spill.
options.why: Only one liquid and one test was done.

options.text: Towel A is the worst brand there is.
options.why: Only three towels were tested.

options.text: In this test, towel B soaked up the most water.
Towel C will always soak up 28 ml.
options.why: Results may change if repeated.

hints: Only claim what the data show.
Compare the three numbers.
Beware of words like always or every.
items.explanation: The results show only that B soaked up the most in this one test. The test cannot support bigger claims.

items.prompt: Joko rolls a toy car down a ramp to see if ramp height changes the distance. Choose 3 things to keep the same.

options.text: The way the car is released

options.why: This is the one thing he is changing.
This is what he measures.

hints: Only one thing is changed.
The rest are controlled.
The height is the variable.
items.explanation: He changes the ramp height, measures the distance, and keeps everything else the same.

items.prompt: Putri times how long a cube melts and gets 41 s once. What is the best way to make her result more reliable?

options.text: Choose the time that looks the nicest.
options.why: This is not scientific.

options.text: Repeat the test several times and find the average.
Use a bigger cube each time.
options.why: Changing the cube makes the test unfair.

options.text: Ask a friend what they think.
options.why: A friend's opinion is not evidence.

hints: One result might be a mistake.
More results help you spot odd ones.
Repeat and average.
items.explanation: Repeating the test several times and averaging gives more reliable results than a single reading.

items.prompt: Five trials of the bubble count are 12, 14, 13, 31, 13. The 31 is anomalous. What is the mean of the other four?
hints: Leave out the anomalous result.
Add the four results.
Divide by 4.

items.prompt: Put the steps of a fair investigation in order.
hints: You ask before you plan.
Collect data before drawing.
The conclusion is last.
items.explanation: Scientists ask a question, predict, plan a fair test, measure, show the data and then conclude.

items.prompt: Match each type of variable to the example in a test on light and plant growth.
pairs: a result that does not fit
a plant 40 cm taller than the rest
hints: Which one does Putri change?
Which one gives the data?
Which one must stay fixed?
items.explanation: The test changes the light, measures the height and keeps the pot the same. A result that does not fit is anomalous.

items.prompt: A result that does not fit the pattern of the other results is called ___.
hints: It is odd one out.
It could be a mistake in measuring.
The word starts with a.
items.explanation: A result that does not fit the pattern is anomalous.

items.prompt: In a school, pupils with bigger shoes also have higher reading scores. A pupil says big feet make you a better reader. What is the most likely reason for the pattern?

options.why: There is no link like this.
Reading does not change the size of feet.

options.text: Older pupils have bigger feet and have also had more time to learn to read.
It is just chance, so it cannot be explained.
options.why: There is a likely third factor.

hints: Both things might depend on something else.
Think about who has bigger feet.
Age affects both.
items.explanation: Age affects both shoe size and reading. A pattern between two things does not prove one causes the other.

items.prompt: True or false: A line graph can show how a measurement changes over time.
hints: What is on the bottom axis?
The line joins points.
It shows change over time.
items.explanation: Points are joined by a line, so you can see patterns such as a steady rise.

items.prompt: True or false: A line of best fit must pass through every point on the graph.
hints: Does measuring ever have tiny errors?
Is the line drawn to follow the pattern?
It goes near the points, not through all.
items.explanation: A line of best fit shows the pattern and passes close to most points. Some points will be a little above or below it because of small errors.

items.prompt: True or false: A result that does not fit the pattern is called an anomalous result.
hints: Does it fit?
What should you do?
Anomalies stand out.
items.explanation: It may be caused by an error, so scientists check it or repeat the test.

items.prompt: True or false: One test is enough evidence to be sure a conclusion is right.
hints: How can you check?
Should you repeat it?
Repeat tests.
items.explanation: Repeating tests and getting similar results makes the evidence more reliable. One result may be a mistake.

items.prompt: What is the mean of 8, 10, 12 and 14?
hints: Add them up first.
The total is 44.
Divide 44 by 4.
items.explanation: 8 plus 10 plus 12 plus 14 is 44. 44 divided by 4 is 11.

items.prompt: Hana measured a bean plant every 5 days. Day 0: 2 cm. Day 5: 6 cm. Day 10: 10 cm. Day 15: 14 cm. Day 20: 18 cm.

parts.prompt: How many cm did it grow every 5 days?
If the pattern continues, how tall on day 25?
What does the graph line look like?

hints: 6 take away 2.
Add the same growth to 18.
It rises by the same amount each time.
items.explanation: It grows 4 cm every 5 days. 18 + 4 = 22 cm. Equal steps make a straight line.
